merged_candidates.anchorage_tie: STAK Energy is headquartered in Anchorage, Alaska per company website (stak.energy states 'Based in Anchorage'); Mahoney's professional profile lists 'Greater Anchorage Area, United States' as location. Founded and runs company from Anchorage. Project site is North Slope but the decision-making and corporate entity are Anchorage-based.

decision.what_happened: The Alaska Department of Natural Resources issued a preliminary decision on May 12, 2026 to lease 715.4 acres of North Slope land to STAK Energy for a proposed $500 million AI and cloud computing data center campus. The DNR determined the project serves the state's 'best interest.' Stak filed the lease application with DNR in November 2025; DNR subsequently solicited competing bids and received none, then moved forward with the preliminary approval. The project would reach up to 3 gigawatts of power capacity, use natural gas for off-grid power generation, and target initial operations by late 2028. A public comment period runs through June 15, 2026.
decision.binary_owned: Mahoney chose to pursue a self-powered, natural-gas-off-grid model for AI data center infrastructure on state-owned North Slope acreage rather than grid-tied or alternative-site approaches, and successfully obtained DNR's preliminary 'best interest' lease determination, committing the company to a 50-year lease track and $500M development path.
decision.ak_consequence: Energy/data infrastructure sector; $500M capital commitment; peak construction workforce of 1,500 jobs and approximately 60 permanent positions; 50-year land lease on North Slope state land; public comment period open through June 15, 2026 with final lease decision pending. Sets precedent for whether Alaska becomes a large-scale AI compute host state using stranded North Slope natural gas.

merged_candidates.prelim_debatable_axis: SHARP, $500M and 50-year state land lease on speculative off-grid natural gas data center model 26 miles from Deadhorse, at the exact moment Cook Inlet gas supply is declining. Stranded North Slope gas plus Arctic free cooling may be a genuine cost advantage for AI compute, but no disclosed outside financing, no anchor tenant, and Mahoney pivoted from a previous crypto mining proposal on the same site.

merged_candidates.role: Senior Vice President of Corporate Development
merged_candidates.anchorage_tie: GCI is Alaska's largest telecommunications provider, headquartered in Anchorage. GCI's network infrastructure and Anchorage operations teams will absorb Quintillion's 1,800+ miles of fiber into GCI's statewide system. Wailand is Anchorage-based and led the acquisition process.

decision.what_happened: GCI Holdings announced it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire 100% of the equity in Quintillion at a $310 million enterprise value. GCI will also reimburse up to $50 million in qualifying capital expenditures for the Nome-to-Homer Express fiber project and provide a $160 million unsecured loan to Quintillion shortly after closing. The transaction combines Quintillion's 1,800+ miles of existing subsea and terrestrial fiber and approximately 1,500 miles of planned fiber expansion with GCI's statewide network.
decision.binary_owned: Approved acquisition. Wailand, as SVP Corporate Development, owns the deal structure and execution of the $310M Quintillion acquisition, the largest Alaska telecom infrastructure transaction in recent years.
decision.ak_consequence: Telecom infrastructure sector; $310M plus $210M in additional capital commitments ($520M total potential outlay); creates a fiber ring around Alaska enabling rerouting during outages; consolidates Alaska's two largest fiber operators; DOD/national security applications cited by Wailand; affects all GCI enterprise and residential customers across Alaska. Closing subject to regulatory approval; timeline 2026 to 2027.

subject_quotes.verbatim: By bringing together complementary fiber routes, deep operational expertise, and long-term investment under one operating model, we're building a network that is stronger, more resilient, and better suited to Alaska's realities than either company could deliver on its own.
subject_quotes.context: Wailand quoted in joint GCI/Quintillion press release announcing definitive acquisition agreement, April 22, 2026

subject_quotes.verbatim: If you can lose those eyes, it immediately becomes a problem. The more resilience that you're building out there, the more useful it is for national security.
subject_quotes.context: Wailand quoted in ADN independent reporting on the acquisition, April 22, 2026, discussing DOD/national security rationale for combined fiber ring

merged_candidates.prelim_debatable_axis: Sharp or wrong depending on framing. GCI consolidating Alaska's two largest fiber operators is either pro-competitive infrastructure build at the scale needed for AI data center workloads, or monopolistic foreclosure of fiber competition in a captive market. The DOD/national security rationale is politically convenient cover. AI angle is INDIRECT (fiber enables AI compute but no AI workload is named in the deal).
merged_candidates.validator_flag: AI angle is indirect. Subject title is M&A leadership, not CTO/CIO.

merged_candidates.role: Assembly Chair (formerly Vice Chair), District 5 West Anchorage
merged_candidates.org: Anchorage Municipal Assembly, Municipality of Anchorage
merged_candidates.anchorage_tie: Bowl-based elected official representing West Anchorage; chairs the governing body of the Municipality of Anchorage.

decision.what_happened: The Anchorage Assembly passed Ordinance AO 2026-27 on an approximately 10-2 vote on March 27, 2026, establishing the first-ever municipal zoning definition for 'data centers' in Anchorage and requiring conditional use permits, utility capacity documentation, 200-foot setbacks from residential areas, and enclosed power equipment for any facility drawing 20 MW or more at peak load. Brawley introduced the ordinance as Assembly Vice Chair and is its named primary sponsor. Brawley was subsequently elected Assembly Chair on April 28, 2026, and made public statements on JBER military data center RFPs on May 5, 2026.
decision.binary_owned: Approved. Brawley sponsored and voted yes on a first-in-Alaska municipal data center zoning framework, restricting AI-era data centers from residential and most commercial zones and requiring grid-capacity sign-off from Chugach Electric before any conditional use permit can advance.
decision.ak_consequence: Energy sector and land use. Any company seeking to site a 20 MW-plus data center within MOA boundaries must now obtain conditional use approval and a signed utility-capacity statement from Chugach Electric. Chugach has publicly stated it currently lacks sufficient gas supply to support large data centers. The ordinance effectively creates a regulatory gate on an estimated $1 to $5 billion class of potential investment.

corroborating_sources.outlet: Davis Wright Tremaine LLP Energy & Environmental Law Blog
Anchorage Daily News (May 5, 2026 follow-up referencing the ordinance as active context)

subject_quotes.verbatim: By learning from other places and emerging best practices around data centers, Anchorage is being proactive and ensuring the right questions are asked during the application process.
subject_quotes.context: Brawley commenting on AO 2026-27 at or around the time of passage, March 27, 2026.

subject_quotes.verbatim: Broadly, I would be hoping that our local leadership has conversations with the Department of Defense, with the entity that would be coming, and with the utility.
subject_quotes.context: Brawley, now Assembly Chair, responding to questions about JBER military data center RFPs in May 2026.

merged_candidates.prelim_debatable_axis: Sharp but arguable. Pro: Anchorage acts before a hyperscale facility locks in, protecting ratepayers and residential neighborhoods. Con: ADN editorial board called it anti-investment signaling; 20 MW threshold could add 12 to 18 months to permitting; JBER sites fall outside MOA jurisdiction anyway.
merged_candidates.in_window_note: PRIMARY DECISION (AO 2026-27 vote) was March 27, 2026, 24 days before window opens. IN-WINDOW DECISIONS: elected Assembly Chair April 28 (in window), May 5 JBER statement (in window). Validator must decide whether to broaden window or use the in-window Chair election + JBER statement as the anchored decision with the March 27 ordinance as context.

merged_candidates.anchorage_tie: Bowl-adjacent elected official representing Eagle River/Chugiak area of the Municipality of Anchorage; decisions affect MOA-wide policy including technology and security infrastructure.

decision.what_happened: The Anchorage Assembly passed Resolution AR 2026-129, sponsored by McCormick along with Vice Chair Daniel Volland and member Yarrow Silvers, expressing the Assembly's 'substantive concerns' about the U.S. Air Force's proposed 7-mile barbed-wire perimeter fence at JBER. The resolution urges JBER to prepare a full Environmental Impact Statement and to extend the public comment period by at least 60 additional days. The draft environmental assessment reviewed by the Assembly explicitly lists motion sensors and surveillance cameras as alternatives to the physical fence that JBER chose not to pursue.
decision.binary_owned: Approved. McCormick sponsored and the Assembly passed a formal resolution opposing JBER's fence-and-no-surveillance-alternative approach, pushing back on a federal security infrastructure decision that had explicitly rejected sensor/camera technology in favor of physical perimeter control.
decision.ak_consequence: Security infrastructure and civil-military relations. The resolution creates a formal municipal record opposing JBER's fence construction timeline, potentially complicating the Air Force's NEPA process and delaying installation. The fence affects wildlife corridors, 12,000+ acres of recreational trails, and moose migration routes adjacent to Anchorage neighborhoods. JBER's public comment period closes May 30, 2026.

corroborating_sources.outlet: Alaska Senate Majority Leader Cathy Giessel newsletter

merged_candidates.prelim_debatable_axis: Mediocre-to-sharp. The AI/surveillance tech angle is thin. The resolution does not itself choose or block surveillance technology. The primary subject is environmental review and public comment, not technology policy.
merged_candidates.validator_flag: Tech angle is thin. Primary subject is environmental review, not AI/data.

decision.what_happened: Tomco's Analytical Science for Environmental Toxicology (ASET) Lab published 'OilSpillNet: A Deep Learning Framework for Accurate Detection and Segmentation of Marine Oil Spills from Imagery' in the Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering, authored by postdoctoral researcher Mohamed Elsheref (lead) and Tomco (supervising PI). decision.binary_owned: Funded/approved. Tomco as ASET Lab Director and supervising PI approved and directed the interdisciplinary pivot to deep learning AI in a traditionally wet-chemistry environmental lab, accepting the Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) grant that funded the work.
decision.ak_consequence: Environmental monitoring sector. Potential deployment of automated, near-real-time oil spill detection in Cook Inlet and Alaska coastal waters, reducing the labor-intensive manual satellite imagery review.

corroborating_sources.outlet: ScienceDirect / Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering (Elsevier)

merged_candidates.prelim_debatable_axis: Sharp with tension. ASET Lab is a wet-chemistry environmental toxicology facility receiving a DFO Canada grant, not an AI lab. Pro: cross-disciplinary AI integration Alaska needs, applied to high-stakes problem. Con: primary funder is Canadian, a postdoc owns the AI architecture, and no Alaska industry partner has been named to deploy OilSpillNet.
merged_candidates.validator_flag: Subject quotes are attributed to Elsheref (the postdoc), not Tomco directly. Only ONE truly independent corroborating source (ScienceDirect listing, paywalled).
